public_rationale: Agents clearly use more tokens than chat. Whether it is "orders of magnitude" depends on the type of agent. For coding agents, a systematic April 2026 study of eight frontier models found about 1,000 times the tokens of code chat. That is three orders of magnitude and supports Marcus. These are the tools at the center of enterprise tokenmaxxing. For agentic workflows in general, Gartner's March 2026 analysis, as reported by DoiT, put it at 5 to 30 times a chatbot query. That is one order of magnitude at most. Anthropic's own 2025 data (4 times for agents, 15 times for multi-agent systems) fits that lower range. So the claim holds for coding agents but overstates the gap for agents in general.
limitations: The result depends on what counts as an "agent" and what baseline is used.
The 1,000x figure is from one preprint on a benchmark, not field data.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: AI agents burn orders of magnitude more tokens than ordinary use, which makes them very costly.

statement.excerpt: Budgets will tighten, especially when people realize just how costly agents (which burn orders of magnitudes more tokens) are.
statement.document_title: Breaking: bad news for three of the biggest IPOs in history

our_interpretation: The comparison baseline is ordinary chat or single-request use of the same models.
"Orders of magnitude" (plural) plainly means roughly 100 times or more. About 10 to 30 times is one order of magnitude at most.
"Agents" is read as AI agents in general, including the coding agents behind most enterprise tokenmaxxing.
The claim is in the present tense, so it describes the state in the months before the 2026-05-28 post.
criteria.support_condition: Measurements from the period showing agents typically use about 100 times or more tokens than chat or single-request use.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Measurements from the period showing agents typically use well under 100 times as many tokens as chat (for example 5 to 30 times).

evidence.locator: section 'Why cost per token measures the wrong thing', paragraph 3
